extracted.intended_audience: programmers/users of the Magma language (students, researchers, computational algebraists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for defining, calling, and debugging functions/procedures in the Magma language, including recursion, forward-declarations, error handling, parameters, assertions, and iterative statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function heading / formal identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: One should begin with a heading that gives Q as the formal identifier: smallest := function(Q)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start a function definition with a clear heading that names the function and lists formal arguments. Examples in the text show 'smallest := function(Q)' and the equivalent func/func-constructor forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a base case in recursive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recursive problem can be solved directly for small inputs (e.g., 'ﬁnding the minimum term of Q is trivial when Q has only one term'), include an explicit base case such as 'if #Q eq 1 then return Q[1];'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The body of recursive functions should begin by handling trivial/small instances to ensure termination; illustrate with smallest(...) where sequence of size 1 is base case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce problem size in recursive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode the recursive insight by reducing the input size (e.g., remove last term, find minimum of remaining sequence, compare using Minimum(a,b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recursive clause should produce a smaller instance that progresses toward the base case; example shows computing prunedmin := $$(Prune(Q)); return Minimum(finalterm, prunedmin);

rubrics_metrics.name: Use $$ inside function expressions for self-reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The $$ sign stands for the function currently being defined; within a function expression the identifier (e.g., smallest) is undeﬁned, so use $$ to refer to the function being defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining recursive functions with func-constructor or function expressions, use $$ rather than the target name because Magma only assigns the name after processing the whole function expression. The $$ symbol is recognized within the func-constructor as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure recursion eventually terminates
rubrics_metrics.description: Recursive functions and procedures must be written with care. The user must ensure that the recursion will eventually terminate, irrespective of the values of the actual arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recursion (including mutual recursion) so that input strictly progresses toward a base case. The text emphasizes termination as a mandatory correctness consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-declaration when referring to not-yet-defined routines
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function/procedure f is about to be defined which invokes an identifier g that has not yet been assigned a function/procedure, type 'forward g;' before defining f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward-declarations indicate to Magma that g will be assigned later. They must occur at main level (not inside another function/procedure). You may declare several names separated by commas (e.g., forward oe, odd, even;). The system expects g to be assigned before invoking f at runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use forward-declarations for mutual recursion and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Two major applications: (1) convenience — allow placing principal programs before helpers; (2) necessity — enable mutually recursive functions/procedures to invoke each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For mutual recursion, forward-declare one name, define the other, then define the forward-declared one. Ensure mutual recursion is designed to terminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function/procedure assignment vs function expression name use
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of 'R := function(...)' you may write 'function R(...)' (function assignment statement). The effect is the same except that inside the function/procedure definition the routine may be called by its name R (rather than $$).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Magma encounters the assignment-form, it internally rewrites instances of the function name within the function expression as $$. Users accustomed to other languages may prefer 'function R(...)' syntax; it allows using R inside the body directly for recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design functions/procedures to handle all input kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Users designing a function or procedure must take care that it can cater for all kinds of input in the actual arguments. Otherwise the behaviour will be unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not handled, the routine may stop with a confusing error, or complete but give wrong results. Anticipate bad types, ranges, and invalid combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use error and error if to provide helpful runtime errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma has an error-statement: 'error expression, ..., expression;' which prints the expressions and breaks out of the call. 'error if condition, expression, ..., expression;' evaluates the condition and acts similarly if condition is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use error to abort with a message and to aid debugging. 'error if' is convenient since it combines the test and the abort. If an error-statement is encountered during a function call, the function does not return a value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check argument types and ranges at call start
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to check the categories of the arguments as soon as execution of the procedure call commences (e.g., ensure Type(c) eq MonStgElt, Type(n) eq RngIntElt, and n in [0..80]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early checks yield clearer, more helpful error messages for callers. Example SepLine uses 'error' or 'error if' to signal bad argument types or out-of-range integers. Also consider checking properties like 'c has only one character'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'error if' for concise checks
rubrics_metrics.description: 'error if' is preferable since this kind of error situation can be detected with a simple test of a condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two equivalent implementations (if... error .../error if ...) are shown; 'error if' is less verbose and clearer for simple precondition checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some runtime errors only found later; make routines robust
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all runtime errors can be found at the beginning of a call; sometimes errors can only be found after several computations have taken place; functions/procedures should be robust enough to deal intelligently with such errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include checks and sensible handling throughout the routine where appropriate; consider intermediate validation where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to user intrinsic simplifies error-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function or procedure is sufficiently useful to be converted into a user intrinsic, certain aspects of error-checking become easier: category-checking of arguments becomes automatic, and there are additional statements for error-handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider making frequently used routines intrinsics to benefit from Magma's built-in argument checking and richer error facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameters are optional arguments with defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameters are like optional arguments, whose purpose is to control some aspect of the algorithm's execution; the algorithm designer must decide a sensible default value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters need only be referred to in calls when the user wishes a non-default value. Parameter names follow identifier rules and have local scope. Online help lists each parameter name, default value, possible values and effect on behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax for parameters in calls
rubrics_metrics.description: The syntax for a call to a function or procedure R that has parameters is: R(arguments : parameter := expr, ..., parameter := expr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All actual value/reference arguments come first, then a colon, then parameter assignments. Only non-default parameters need to be listed (though listing defaults is permitted). The order of parameter assignments is not important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameters control function behaviour (understand allowed values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameters may take discrete named values affecting behaviour (e.g., IsSubsequence's Kind parameter default "Consecutive"; other values include "Sequential" and "Setwise").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the meaning of each parameter value; if a non-default mode is needed specify 'Kind := "Sequential"' etc. Illegal parameter values should be detected and reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose parameter vs value argument by default usability
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision as to whether a setting should be a parameter or a value argument depends on whether a default value can be found for it that would be the desired value most of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If most calls need a particular value, make it the parameter default; otherwise consider making it an explicit value argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax for parameters in definitions (defaults assigned)
rubrics_metrics.description: In function/procedure definitions, follow formal arguments with a colon and a comma-separated list of parameter assignments; the assigned values are the defaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SeparatingBlock := procedure(k : c := "*", n := 60) assigns default values for parameters c and n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameters for algorithm selection and tuning
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameters may control which algorithm is used and algorithm-specific bounds (e.g., Factor(n : Al := "Division", Lower := 2, Upper := min(Lower+1000,n))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set sensible defaults for algorithmic parameters; document how changing them affects performance and results. If an algorithm choice ignores some parameters, note that in documentation or checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check legality of parameter values in function body
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions should test that parameter values are legal (e.g., error if Category(n) ne RngIntElt or n lt 1, "Error: n not a positive integer"; error if Al notin {"Trapezoid","Simpson"}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate parameters at start of function and provide informative error messages for illegal values; examples given for quadrature function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use assert to encode invariants and internal correctness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: assert condition; checks a Boolean at runtime: if true nothing happens; if false Magma stops execution and gives an assertion failed error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assert inside functions/procedures to express facts that must hold at that program point (e.g., after computing gcd by algorithm, assert g eq GCD(a,b)). Assertions can be disabled globally with SetAssertions(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertions can be globally enabled/disabled
rubrics_metrics.description: GetAssertions() returns whether assertions are checked (default true). SetAssertions(b) can change this; if set to false Magma ignores assert-statements entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assertions during development to catch errors; disable in production if slight performance improvements are needed and invariants are trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constructors over explicit loops when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma’s set and sequence constructors allow many iteration processes to be expressed statically; Magma style favours constructors over iterative statements when the task is relatively simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructors are often more concise and readable (example: PrimesCubed := { p^3 : p in [1..20] | IsPrime(p) }). Use explicit iteration when there are many auxiliary identifiers, complex operations, or many print statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand three iteration forms and their termination modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma has three forms of iterative statements: the for-statement (iteration over a predetermined domain), the while-statement (Boolean tested at beginning of each loop), and the repeat-statement (Boolean tested at end of each loop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also use break for immediate termination and continue to end current loop iteration. Choose the form that matches the intended termination condition (domain-based vs condition-based start/end).

rubrics_metrics.name: While-statement semantics and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax: 'while Boolean expression do statements end while;'. The Boolean expression is evaluated at the beginning of each loop; if it is already false the body is not executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there is at least one statement in the body. Use while when zero or more iterations are acceptable depending on initial condition. Example: computing factorial by decrementing a counter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat-statement semantics and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntax: 'repeat statements until Boolean expression;'. The termination condition is tested at the end of each loop so the body is always executed at least once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeat when at least one pass is required (e.g., testing Fermat numbers starting with n=1). Combine multiple conditions with 'or'/'and' as needed for composite stopping criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: For-statement semantics and syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: General structure: 'for identifier in domain do statements end for;'. The loop identifier takes elements of the domain in succession and the body executes for each value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for when the iteration domain is predetermined and you want each domain element visited exactly once in order. Domains can be sequences, sets, ranges, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative statement construction and editing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When an iterative statement is typed into Magma, if the system detects an error before the end of the whole statement has been reached, the part of the statement already typed is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For longer iterative statements, develop them in an external file and load into Magma (see Section 14.2). The system may give a special prompt while entering multi-line loops; examples show 'while>' prompt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile with time to compare algorithm performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma’s time command prints CPU seconds taken to execute a statement (e.g., 'time fibonacciA := fiboA(L); Time: 2.919').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time to compare algorithms' execution times; choose implementations considering development time, readability, and execution time.
